The long history of the scroll bar

By Ada Lovelace

The scroll bar is the oldest piece of furniture in the graphical interface, and almost nobody looks at it on purpose. It began as a way to say where you were in a document that was longer than the screen, and it has been quietly saying the same thing ever since, through every change of fashion in the decoration around it.

Early systems drew the bar as a column of pixels with a box inside it, and the box was the document. Dragging the box moved the view; clicking above or below it moved the view by a page. The metaphor was so direct that it needed no explanation, and so it survived the arrival of the mouse wheel, the trackpad, and the touch screen, each of which made the bar less necessary and none of which replaced it.

The argument for hiding the bar is that it takes space and repeats what the content already says. The argument against hiding it is that a reader who cannot see the bar cannot tell how much is left, and a reader who cannot tell how much is left reads differently: faster, with less patience, and with a worse sense of the shape of the thing being read.

Modern systems compromise. The bar fades away while the page is still, and returns the moment a finger or a wheel moves, which gives the space back without giving up the signal. It is a reasonable trade, and it depends on the reader noticing the bar in the half second it is visible, which is a lot to ask of a piece of furniture nobody looks at on purpose.

What the bar has never managed is to say anything about the content it measures. It reports a position and a proportion, and it is silent about sections, headings, figures, and everything else a reader might navigate by. Every attempt to make it say more — marks for search results, colours for changed lines, thumbnails of pages — has been useful in one application and ignored in the rest.

So the scroll bar remains what it was: a thin, honest answer to a question the reader keeps asking. There are better answers, and none of them is as cheap.
